title: CACFG: Curvature-Aware Classifier-Free Guidance and Optimal Control

paper.title: CACFG: Curvature-Aware Classifier-Free Guidance and Optimal Control
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models generate samples by learning to reverse a fixed corruption process, and classifier-free guidance (CFG) is the standard mechanism for conditioning this process on a desired class or prompt. CFG can be applied at varying guidance strengths, and while higher strengths improve image quality and conditional alignment, too high a guidance strength can degrade image quality and diversity. Furthermore, CFG violates principled diffusion sampling dynamics, and existing explanations for why it works despite the violation disagree on the underlying theory or do not extend to deterministic samplers used in practice. We address both these issues. We first frame CFG sampling as a continuous-time optimal control problem, treating the sampling trajectory as a sequence of controls chosen to maximise the probability of the desired condition. Solving the resulting Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation shows that CFG is recovered under specific path costs when using an unconstrained control set. We argue this lack of constraint is responsible for CFG’s failure at high guidance strengths, since it permits the sampling path to move arbitrarily far from the current image estimate. To fix this, we propose curvature-aware CFG (CACFG), which constrains the control set to a hypersphere informed by the Gaussian regularisation used when training variational autoencoders. We show that the control inputs produced by CFG sampling routinely violate this bound, and that across diffusion models, datasets, and guidance schedules, CACFG achieves superior generative quality at mid-to-high guidance strengths with a less severe quality-diversity tradeoff than regular CFG.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models generate samples by learning to iteratively reverse a fixed process that gradually corrupts data with noise ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ) . Classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) provides a mechanism to control the content of generated images by using a variable guidance strength parameter to target a tilted conditional distribution. However, this tilted distribution is not the marginal of any true diffusion process, and excessive CFG guidance can reduce image diversity and degrade image quality by introducing visual artefacts ( Sadat et al., 2025 ; Karras et al., 2024 ) . Despite this, CFG is frequently used in practice, and practitioners select the largest guidance strengths that do not harm image quality ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ; Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) . Previous work has proposed methods of fixing CFG artefacts: CFG++ ( Chung et al., 2025 ) and Interval-CFG (IntCFG) ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) each attribute CFG’s artefacts to the sampling trajectory departing the image manifold, correcting for this by varying guidance strength across the trajectory. A separate line of work asks why CFG works despite violating diffusion sampling dynamics. Hypotheses attribute its effectiveness to a shared bias in the conditional and unconditional denoisers ( Karras et al., 2024 ) , an implicit correction for the poorly-approximated tilted distribution ( Moufad et al., 2025 ) , or an equivalence with a predictor-corrector scheme in the continuous-time SDE limit ( Bradley & Nakkiran, 2025 ) . However, these explanations disagree on the mechanism responsible, and they do not rigorously extend to commonly used deterministic samplers. We address this gap by reformulating CFG sampling as a continuous-time optimal control problem: rather than fixing the sampling trajectory as a function of stochastic transition kernels, we treat it as a sequence of controls chosen to maximise the terminal reward p ⁡ ( ξ ∣ 𝒙 0 ) p(\xi\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{0}) , i.e., how probable it is that the sample is of the desired condition/class ξ \xi . Solving the resulting Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation shows that the optimal control recovers CFG when the control set is unconstrained and the traversal penalty is expressed in the same scale as the diffusion training loss. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to frame CFG as a deterministic optimal control problem in this way. Additionally, existing guidance scheduling methods such as CFG++ and IntCFG also emerge from this same optimal control formulation under alternative choices of the traversal penalty (Appendix B ). By examining the path costs of this optimisation problem, we find that the CFG diffusion sampling trajectory is encouraged to: align the conditional and CFG scores at early-to-mid sampling times; converge towards a local maximum at late sampling times; and avoid traversing near a maximum too early. This provides significant insight into how CFG works, and why it exhibits certain pathologies. Our optimal control formulation shows that traditional CFG imposes no constraint on the control set. This permits the sampling path to move arbitrarily far from the current image estimate given sufficiently low traversal penalty. We argue this is directly responsible for CFG’s failure modes in high-guidance regimes. To address this, we propose a constrained control set and corresponding curvature-aware CFG scheme (CACFG) that relies on a property latent diffusion models have by construction: the training objective of their variational autoencoder (VAE) is explicitly regularised towards an isotropic Gaussian. We hypothesise that this forces most encodings to lie within a hypersphere of an estimable radius, and we show empirically that the Tweedie estimates produced by traditional CFG sampling frequently violate this theoretical upper bound, while those of CACFG do not (Figure 1 ). We find that across diffusion models, datasets, and guidance schedules, CACFG has superior generative quality at mid-to-high guidance strengths as measured by various quality metrics. Our core contributions are as follows: (i) We show that diffusion guidance can be interpreted as a continuous-time control problem; (ii) We show that classifier-free guidance (CFG) is one solution to this control problem, and that existing guidance scheduling methods, such as CFG++ ( Chung et al., 2025 ) and IntCFG ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) , arise from the same framework under alternative choices of the traversal penalty; (iii) We propose a method of using the Gaussian regularisation term of the VAE training loss to infer the structure of the embedded image manifold; (iv) We propose a constrained control set for the continuous-time optimisation problem that results in a diffusion guidance (CACFG) that provides superior conditional generation with a less severe quality-diversity tradeoff than unconstrained guidance methods, at negligible additional computational cost.

sections.heading: 3 Related Work
sections.text: Chung et al. (2025) attributes CFG artefacts such as colour oversaturation and broken invertibility to an off-manifold effect: since ω > 1 \omega>1 extrapolates beyond the conditional and unconditional denoiser outputs, the resulting noise estimate can fall off the data manifold. By reformulating guidance as a manifold-constrained score-matching problem, Chung et al. (2025) appeal to the linear manifold hypothesis ( Chung et al., 2022 ) to compute a manifold constrained gradient to force the sample to remain on the theorised linear image manifold. Alternatively, Interval-CFG (IntCFG) ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) hypothesises that CFG artefacts can be attributed to when guidance is applied: guidance at high noise levels collapses diversity by prematurely committing the trajectory to a small set of modes, while guidance at low noise levels has minimal effect. Thus, IntCFG disables guidance outside an interval of intermediate noise levels. Though motivated differently, both methods let the guidance scale of ( 8 ) vary across the sampling trajectory, a fact we make concrete in Appendix B . Alternatively, techniques such as Adaptive Projected Guidance (APG) ( Sadat et al., 2025 ) reshape the CFG update itself. However, none of this work provides a rigorous explanation as to why CFG is able to generate conditional images, despite violating diffusion sampling dynamics. Karras et al. (2024) attributes CFG’s effectiveness to a shared model bias: a capacity-limited denoiser over-covers sparsely populated regions of the data manifold, and because the unconditional model exhibits this bias more severely than the conditional one, their ratio acts as an attractive force that pulls samples towards the image manifold. Moufad et al. (2025) show that the tilted distribution of ( 6 ) can be recovered by augmenting CFG with a corrective Rényi-divergence term, and they argue that CFG is just poorly approximating the true tilted distribution. Bradley & Nakkiran (2025) instead prove that in the continuous-time SDE limit, the stochastic (DDPM) variant ( Ho et al., 2020 ) of CFG is identical to a predictor-corrector scheme that pairs DDIM ( Song et al., 2021a ) denoising with a Langevin-dynamics corrector on the tilted distribution. However, this does not account for deterministic (flow ODE) variants of CFG, and the explanations of Karras et al. (2024) and Moufad et al. (2025) disagree on the key mechanisms.

Compensating for weak class adherence with a large guidance scale ω \omega (or small r ⁡ ( s ) r(s) ) may move the sampling trajectory into regions with few training samples, and thus, require the model to extrapolate. This is a known failure mode of neural networks–adversarial regions populate extrapolated sections of the learned manifold, and they cause networks to behave erratically ( Szegedy et al., 2014 ; Goodfellow et al., 2015 ; Madry et al., 2018 ) . sections.heading: 6 CACFG Experiments
sections.text: Diffusion models. We evaluate CACFG using two latent diffusion models of varying sizes: Stable Diffusion 1.5 (SD1.5) ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) and Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) ( Podell et al., 2024 ) . Both are text-conditioned latent diffusion models that run the diffusion of ( 1 ) on a VAE latent space trained using the same objective of ( 9 ). SD1.5 and SDXL have differing generative resolutions of 512 × \times 512 and 1024 × \times 1024, which have substantially different compute costs. Thus, for SD1.5 experiments we generate 10,000 samples for each guidance-dataset-strength setting, while for SDXL we generate 2,000. We run both models on a NVIDIA RTX4090, and the curvature-aware projection does not incur substantive compute overhead–all models run at their originally reported speeds. Datasets. We generate images conditioned on two datasets: ImageNet ( Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) , which provides class-conditional generation across 1000 object categories, and COCO ( Lin et al., 2014 ) , which provides caption-conditioned generation–a more sophisticated generative task. Guidance schedules. We compare three guidance-weight schedules ω ⁡ ( t ) \omega(t) : the constant-weight CFG of ( 8 ) ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , and the two scheduled alternatives CFG++ ( Chung et al., 2025 ) and IntCFG ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) , whose exact forms are given in Appendix B . Each schedule is evaluated both on its own and combined with the curvature-aware control set of ( 23 ), giving the CACFG, CACFG++, and IntCACFG guidance schemes respectively. Across all curvature-aware variants we fix the confidence level of ( 21 ) at p = 0.95 p=0.95 , which corresponds to r u = 129.16 r_{u}=129.16 and r u = 257.16 r_{u}=257.16 for SD1.5 and SDXL, respectively. Based on initial ablations (Appendix C.3 ), we use the blending parameter γ = 0.5 \gamma=0.5 and γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 for SD1.5 and SDXL, respectively. Additionally, we use the DDIM ODE solver ( Song et al., 2021a ) for SD1.5 and SDXL, as it is the most common deterministic solver. Guidance weights. We report the guidance weight of CFG and compute an approximate equivalent weight under each other schedule. That is, we find schedule parameters, θ \theta , such that ∫ 0 T ω CFG ​ 𝑑 t = ∫ 0 T ω ⁡ ( t , θ ) ​ 𝑑 t \int_{0}^{T}\omega_{\text{CFG}}dt=\int_{0}^{T}\omega(t;\theta)dt . This compares schedules with equal approximate total path perturbations. For SD1.5 we use CFG weights ω CFG = 5 , 7.5 , 10 , 15 \omega_{\text{CFG}}=5,7.5,10,15 , and for SDXL we use ω CFG = 10 , 15 , 20 , 25 \omega_{\text{CFG}}=10,15,20,25 . This discrepancy arises because SDXL is significantly more resistant to excessive CFG guidance, making comparisons at lower guidance strengths less meaningful. Metrics. We report nine metrics measuring image quality across varying axes. Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) ( Heusel et al., 2018 ) measures the similarity of real and generated image distributions. Density and Coverage ( Naeem et al., 2020 ) report the fidelity and diversity of the generated images by comparing manifolds fitted to real and generated images. NIQE ( Mittal et al., 2013 ) , BRISQUE ( Mittal et al., 2012 ) , and TReS ( Golestaneh et al., 2022 ) are no-reference perceptual quality metrics, scoring an image’s naturalness based on its pixel statistics. CLIP score ( Radford et al., 2021 ) measures prompt alignment via the cosine similarity between a generated image’s CLIP embedding and its conditioning. Human Preference Score v2 (HPSv2) ( Wu et al., 2023 ) is a model trained to mimic human rankings of image quality. We note that HPSv2 and CLIP score are known to artificially improve at large CFG strengths despite poorer image quality and increasing saturation ( Xie et al., 2026 ) . We therefore additionally report Saturation ( Sadat et al., 2025 ) , computed as the mean of the saturation channel after converting each image from RGB to HSV, to measure this effect.

sections.heading: 6.1 Results
sections.text: Distribution quality and diversity. When using SD1.5 we find FID, Density, and Coverage are improved or equivalent under the curvature-aware (CA) correction for all three guidance schedules and both datasets, with the gap widening substantially at higher guidance strengths (Figures 2 and 6 ). Since Density and Coverage improve alongside FID rather than trading off against it, the corrected samples are more accurately contained within the real-image manifold and also cover a wider region of it, indicating an improvement in both quality and diversity. Figure 2: Performance of CFG, CFG++, and IntCFG with (solid line) and without (dotted line) our curvature-aware correction using SD1.5 on COCO. Some metric axes have been flipped so that the improvement direction is vertically up the page. Zoom in for easier viewing. The same pattern holds for SDXL (Figure 7 ); however, Density and Coverage also depend on guidance strength in a way they do not for SD1.5. At the lowest guidance strength tested, we find both Density and Coverage are marginally degraded by the CA correction, before favouring the correction from moderate guidance strengths onward, alongside a FID advantage that similarly grows across the same range. We hypothesise two explanations for this phenomenon. First, SDXL is a higher-capacity model and is more robust to the manifold departures, thus, the CA control set has less to correct at low guidance, and its benefit only becomes apparent once uncorrected guidance has sufficiently corrupted the sampling trajectory. Second, at low guidance strengths the more restrictive control constraint, U γ ​ ( t ) U_{\gamma}(t) , limits the sampler’s ability to search the latent space, a cost that is outweighed once the guidance strength (effective search budget) is high enough. Thus, across both SD1.5 and SDXL, the CA correction provides superior conditional generation at moderate-to-high guidance strengths, with a less severe quality-diversity tradeoff than that exhibited by unconstrained guidance methods. These findings are supported qualitatively by the samples in Figure 3 and Appendix D.2 . CFG CACFG Figure 3: Comparison of CFG ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) and CACFG (ours) at guidance strength ω = 15 \omega=15 on the COCO ( Lin et al., 2014 ) dataset. CACFG better preserves fine detail: the middle image has a correctly numbered clock face, while the rightmost image reconstructs Van Gogh’s The Starry Night . Perceptual quality. NIQE, BRISQUE, and TReS all favour the curvature-aware variants at every guidance strength for both SD1.5 and SDXL, with the largest gains at high guidance. As these are no-reference measures of image pixel statistics, this indicates that curvature-aware guidance produces images with more natural low-level statistics, independently of any comparison to the real data distribution, and that this benefit is consistent across model scale, guidance schedule, and diffusion model. Prompt alignment. CLIP score improves only marginally under ImageNet but more substantially under COCO, for both SD1.5 and SDXL. We hypothesise that ImageNet’s single-object class prompts are simple enough that standard guidance can satisfy them at these guidance strengths, leaving no room for the CA correction to help, whereas COCO’s complex caption prompts are harder to satisfy: by keeping the sampling trajectory closer to the latent image manifold, curvature-aware guidance allows higher guidance strengths to be spent productively toward matching the full caption, rather than being wasted on manifold-departing artefacts. Human-preference metrics and saturation. HPSv2 is the one metric where the curvature-aware variants are outperformed by their uncorrected counterparts, an effect that is mild for SD1.5 but more pronounced for SDXL. However, the Saturation values of both Figures 6 and 7 show that this coincides with increasing saturation levels, while curvature-aware guidance keeps saturation roughly constant. Given that Xie et al. (2026) have shown HPSv2 and CLIP scores artificially increase alongside saturation, and that every other image-quality metric favours the curvature-aware correction for both models, we interpret the higher HPSv2 of uncorrected guidance as an instance of this failure mode rather than a quality advantage.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We show via the HJB equation that CFG and other guidance schedules can be derived as the optimal control for a continuous-time optimisation problem. Existing CFG corrections assume the underlying image manifold has some known geometry, but this is not guaranteed for latent diffusion models, whose latent image manifold is governed by what the VAE has learned. We use the Gaussian regularisation term of the VAE loss to infer that most image encodings lie within a hypersphere of estimable radius. We then propose a curvature-aware CFG correction that constrains the control set of our optimisation problem to a time-varying hypersphere whose radius is informed by the estimated radius. We find that at high guidance scales this generates images with substantially better quality, as measured by FID, NIQE, BRISQUE, TReS, Density, and Coverage. Thus, our constrained guidance provides superior conditional generation with a less severe quality-diversity tradeoff than that exhibited by unconstrained guidance methods, and functionally no additional compute cost.

sections.heading: A.1 Limitations
sections.text: We note three limitations of our work, each of which we view as a promising direction for future work rather than a fundamental shortcoming of the proposed optimal control framework. First, the control set U γ ​ ( t ) U_{\gamma}(t) we optimise over is time-varying but not state-varying; extending it to depend jointly on sampling time and the current state 𝒙 t \boldsymbol{x}_{t} would more directly incentivise training a model to perform the image-manifold projection. Second, our optimal control perspective does not currently explain guidance techniques such as APG ( Sadat et al., 2025 ) , which act by manipulating the guidance gradient itself, rather than by reweighting it through the guidance schedule. Finally, our formulation is posed for deterministic sampling processes, and does not immediately extend to stochastic samplers. However, these extensions are unnecessary for understanding and improving traditional classifier-free guidance on deterministic samplers, which was the primary objective of this work.

sections.heading: A.2 Reproducibility
sections.text: We ensure reproducibility by providing a detailed description of our algorithm in the main text (Algorithm 1 ). Additionally, our code and the configuration files necessary to replicate our experiments are made publicly available. Comparison methods are implemented using default parameters or with parameters selected based on the respective authors’ tuning algorithms.

sections.heading: A.3 AI use
sections.text: We used large language models as a writing and verification aid during the preparation of this paper. Specifically, AI assistance was used to check and typeset proofs that we had already derived by hand, to edit and improve the clarity of rough prose drafts, and to assist with LaTeX formatting of figures. AI assistance was not used to write experiment code, nor to generate the ideas, methods, or theoretical contributions presented in this work; all such content originates from the authors.

sections.heading: C.3 Curvature-aware upper bound blending parameter
sections.text: The blending parameter γ \gamma interpolates between the two extremes of the Gaussian hypothesis underlying U γ ​ ( t ) U_{\gamma}(t) : at γ = 0 \gamma=0 the control set assumes the hypothesis holds exactly, while at γ = 1 \gamma=1 it retains only the raw upper bound r u r_{u} ( 23 ). We sweep γ ∈ { 0.0 , 0.1 , … , 1.0 } \gamma\in\{0.0,0.1,\dots,1.0\} for CACFG on ImageNet, for both SD1.5 (Table 2 ) and SDXL (Table 3 ). A consistent pattern emerges across both models: loosening the control set steadily improves prompt alignment and human-preference scores (CLIP, HPSv2) and steadily increases saturation, while the remaining fidelity metrics (FID, NIQE, BRISQUE, Density, Coverage) improve sharply over the first few steps of the sweep and then plateau. No single value of γ \gamma is simultaneously optimal across every metric, so selecting γ \gamma requires an explicit choice about how to balance prompt alignment against the residual fidelity cost of moving away from γ = 0.0 \gamma=0.0 ; we describe that choice, and its cost, for each model below. For SD1.5, we select γ = 0.5 \gamma=0.5 . At this value, six of the nine metrics (NIQE, BRISQUE, Density, Coverage, CLIP, and HPSv2) sit within 1 % 1\% of the best value achieved anywhere in the sweep, and FID ( 14.97 14.97 ) is close to its sweep-best ( 14.53 14.53 ) and far below the γ = 0.0 \gamma=0.0 value ( 16.95 16.95 ). Beyond γ = 0.5 \gamma=0.5 , prompt-alignment and preference gains diminish sharply: CLIP and HPSv2 each move by less than 0.15 % 0.15\% between γ = 0.5 \gamma=0.5 and γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 . Over the same range, the two metrics that continue to degrade past γ = 0.5 \gamma=0.5 worsen further: TReS, which peaks early at γ = 0.1 \gamma=0.1 and declines steadily thereafter, falling below even its γ = 0.0 \gamma=0.0 value; and saturation, which increases monotonically with γ \gamma throughout the sweep. We therefore treat γ = 0.5 \gamma=0.5 as close to the point of diminishing returns for SD1.5: it captures nearly all of the available prompt-alignment gain without paying the additional TReS and saturation cost of continuing to γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 . For SDXL, we instead select γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 . Unlike SD1.5, fidelity metrics for SDXL plateau from roughly γ = 0.3 \gamma=0.3 – 0.4 0.4 onward and remain within a small margin of their sweep-best all the way to γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 . FID, TReS, Density, and Coverage are each within 2 % 2\% of their respective optima at γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 , while CLIP and HPSv2 are both maximised at γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 . This is consistent with our hypothesis that SDXL, as a higher-capacity model, is more robust to the manifold departure the curvature-aware correction addresses, and so tolerates a looser control set with comparatively little fidelity cost. The corresponding cost is a mild increase in BRISQUE ( 2.7 % 2.7\% above its sweep-best) and saturation, which reaches its highest value in the sweep at γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 ; we accept this cost given the consistent, and in several cases maximal, gains elsewhere. sections.text: Optimal control problem and HJB equation: We first fix our notation for the optimal control problem underlying the HJB equation, following the general formulation of Berkovitz & Medhin (2012) (§2.3, pp. 19–21) and Liberzon (2012) (§5.1.2, pp. 158–159), generalising the control constraint set to vary with time as in Berkovitz & Medhin (2012) (§6.2, p. 150). Problem E.5 (Optimal Control Problem) . Fix t l < T t_{l}<T . Let 𝐱 t ∈ ℝ m \boldsymbol{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} for t ∈ [ t l , T ] t\in[t_{l},T] , let 𝐮 t ∈ U ⁡ ( t ) ⊆ ℝ p \boldsymbol{u}_{t}\in U(t)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p} be a control taking values in a nonempty, time-varying control set U ⁡ ( t ) U(t) , and let 𝐛 : ℝ × ℝ m × ℝ p → ℝ m \boldsymbol{b}:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{p}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} . CFG can be applied at varying guidance strengths, and while higher strengths improve image quality and conditional alignment, too high a guidance strength can degrade image quality and diversity. Furthermore, CFG violates principled diffusion sampling dynamics, and existing explanations for why it works despite the violation disagree on the underlying theory or do not extend to deterministic samplers used in practice. We address both these issues. We first frame CFG sampling as a continuous-time optimal control problem, treating the sampling trajectory as a sequence of controls chosen to maximise the probability of the desired condition. Solving the resulting Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation shows that CFG is recovered under specific path costs when using an unconstrained control set. We argue this lack of constraint is responsible for CFG’s failure at high guidance strengths, since it permits the sampling path to move arbitrarily far from the current image estimate. To fix this, we propose curvature-aware CFG (CACFG), which constrains the control set to a hypersphere informed by the Gaussian regularisation used when training variational autoencoders. We show that the control inputs produced by CFG sampling routinely violate this bound, and that across diffusion models, datasets, and guidance schedules, CACFG achieves superior generative quality at mid-to-high guidance strengths with a less severe quality-diversity tradeoff than regular CFG. 1 Introduction Diffusion models generate samples by learning to iteratively reverse a fixed process that gradually corrupts data with noise ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ) . Classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) provides a mechanism to control the content of generated images by using a variable guidance strength parameter to target a tilted conditional distribution. However, this tilted distribution is not the marginal of any true diffusion process, and excessive CFG guidance can reduce image diversity and degrade image quality by introducing visual artefacts ( Sadat et al., 2025 ; Karras et al., 2024 ) . Despite this, CFG is frequently used in practice, and practitioners select the largest guidance strengths that do not harm image quality ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ; Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) . Previous work has proposed methods of fixing CFG artefacts: CFG++ ( Chung et al., 2025 ) and Interval-CFG (IntCFG) ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) each attribute CFG’s artefacts to the sampling trajectory departing the image manifold, correcting for this by varying guidance strength across the trajectory. A separate line of work asks why CFG works despite violating diffusion sampling dynamics. Hypotheses attribute its effectiveness to a shared bias in the conditional and unconditional denoisers ( Karras et al., 2024 ) , an implicit correction for the poorly-approximated tilted distribution ( Moufad et al., 2025 ) , or an equivalence with a predictor-corrector scheme in the continuous-time SDE limit ( Bradley & Nakkiran, 2025 ) . However, these explanations disagree on the mechanism responsible, and they do not rigorously extend to commonly used deterministic samplers. We address this gap by reformulating CFG sampling as a continuous-time optimal control problem: rather than fixing the sampling trajectory as a function of stochastic transition kernels, we treat it as a sequence of controls chosen to maximise the terminal reward p ⁡ ( ξ ∣ 𝒙 0 ) p(\xi\mid oldsymbol{x}_{0}) , i.e., how probable it is that the sample is of the desired condition/class ξ \xi . Solving the resulting Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation shows that the optimal control recovers CFG when the control set is unconstrained and the traversal penalty is expressed in the same scale as the diffusion training loss. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to frame CFG as a deterministic optimal control problem in this way. Additionally, existing guidance scheduling methods such as CFG++ and IntCFG also emerge from this same optimal control formulation under alternative choices of the traversal penalty (Appendix B ). By examining the path costs of this optimisation problem, we find that the CFG diffusion sampling trajectory is encouraged to: align the conditional and CFG scores at early-to-mid sampling times; converge towards a local maximum at late sampling times; and avoid traversing near a maximum too early. This provides significant insight into how CFG works, and why it exhibits certain pathologies. Our optimal control formulation shows that traditional CFG imposes no constraint on the control set. This permits the sampling path to move arbitrarily far from the current image estimate given sufficiently low traversal penalty. We argue this is directly responsible for CFG’s failure modes in high-guidance regimes. To address this, we propose a constrained control set and corresponding curvature-aware CFG scheme (CACFG) that relies on a property latent diffusion models have by construction: the training objective of their variational autoencoder (VAE) is explicitly regularised towards an isotropic Gaussian. We hypothesise that this forces most encodings to lie within a hypersphere of an estimable radius, and we show empirically that the Tweedie estimates produced by traditional CFG sampling frequently violate this theoretical upper bound, while those of CACFG do not (Figure 1 ). We find that across diffusion models, datasets, and guidance schedules, CACFG has superior generative quality at mid-to-high guidance strengths as measured by various quality metrics. Our core contributions are as follows: (i) We show that diffusion guidance can be interpreted as a continuous-time control problem; (ii) We show that classifier-free guidance (CFG) is one solution to this control problem, and that existing guidance scheduling methods, such as CFG++ ( Chung et al., 2025 ) and IntCFG ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) , arise from the same framework under alternative choices of the traversal penalty; (iii) We propose a method of using the Gaussian regularisation term of the VAE training loss to infer the structure of the embedded image manifold; (iv) We propose a constrained control set for the continuous-time optimisation problem that results in a diffusion guidance (CACFG) that provides superior conditional generation with a less severe quality-diversity tradeoff than unconstrained guidance methods, at negligible additional computational cost. 2 Preliminaries Denoising diffusion models generate data by learning to reverse a fixed diffusion (noising) process. (2025) attributes CFG artefacts such as colour oversaturation and broken invertibility to an off-manifold effect: since ω > 1 \omega>1 extrapolates beyond the conditional and unconditional denoiser outputs, the resulting noise estimate can fall off the data manifold. By reformulating guidance as a manifold-constrained score-matching problem, Chung et al. (2025) appeal to the linear manifold hypothesis ( Chung et al., 2022 ) to compute a manifold constrained gradient to force the sample to remain on the theorised linear image manifold. Alternatively, Interval-CFG (IntCFG) ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) hypothesises that CFG artefacts can be attributed to when guidance is applied: guidance at high noise levels collapses diversity by prematurely committing the trajectory to a small set of modes, while guidance at low noise levels has minimal effect. Thus, IntCFG disables guidance outside an interval of intermediate noise levels. Though motivated differently, both methods let the guidance scale of ( 8 ) vary across the sampling trajectory, a fact we make concrete in Appendix B . Alternatively, techniques such as Adaptive Projected Guidance (APG) ( Sadat et al., 2025 ) reshape the CFG update itself. However, none of this work provides a rigorous explanation as to why CFG is able to generate conditional images, despite violating diffusion sampling dynamics. Karras et al. (2024) attributes CFG’s effectiveness to a shared model bias: a capacity-limited denoiser over-covers sparsely populated regions of the data manifold, and because the unconditional model exhibits this bias more severely than the conditional one, their ratio acts as an attractive force that pulls samples towards the image manifold. Moufad et al. (2025) show that the tilted distribution of ( 6 ) can be recovered by augmenting CFG with a corrective Rényi-divergence term, and they argue that CFG is just poorly approximating the true tilted distribution. Bradley & Nakkiran (2025) instead prove that in the continuous-time SDE limit, the stochastic (DDPM) variant ( Ho et al., 2020 ) of CFG is identical to a predictor-corrector scheme that pairs DDIM ( Song et al., 2021a ) denoising with a Langevin-dynamics corrector on the tilted distribution. However, this does not account for deterministic (flow ODE) variants of CFG, and the explanations of Karras et al. (2024) and Moufad et al.
